cards.explanation: The answer is False. Shechem doesn't walk away. The text says, “And his soul was drawn to Dinah, the daughter of Jacob. He loved the young girl and spoke to her tenderly.” That doesn't wipe out what he did in verse 2, and the text never says it does. It just tells us what Shechem, the prince of the region, felt and did next.
The answer is “Get me this girl as a wife.” Shechem tells his father Hamor that, friends. He takes the request to his dad and asks for a marriage. Then Hamor comes to speak with Jacob.

The answer is that Jacob stays silent until his sons return. Jacob heard the news, but since his sons were with his livestock in the field, “…he remained silent about it until they returned.” I think that was a heavy wait for a father. Meanwhile, Hamor came to speak with him.
The answer is fury. The text says Jacob's sons “…were filled with grief and fury…” Both of those come together in one verse, friends. This is where the story starts to boil.

The answer is True. The text says Shechem “…had committed an outrage in Israel by lying with Jacob’s daughter…” and ends with “…a thing that should not be done.” Verse 2 says plainly that he “…took her and lay with her by force.” The text doesn't soften it, and neither will I.

The answer is to intermarry and settle in the land. Hamor says, “Intermarry with us; give us your daughters and take our daughters for yourselves.” Then he adds, “You may settle among us, and the land will be open to you.” That's a whole package deal, friends: marriage, neighbors and room to grow.

The answer is every male in the city. The brothers say the condition is that “…you become circumcised like us…” and then add, “…every one of your males.” Remember, the text already told us they answered deceitfully. Keep that in your back pocket, friends.

The answer is True. The brothers say, “We will dwell among you and become one people.” That's what they say to Hamor and Shechem. But the text has already told us the sons answered deceitfully. So listen to this offer with that in mind.

The answer is that they'll take their sister and go. If Hamor's men won't be circumcised, the brothers say, “…then we will take our sister and go.” It's the other side of their offer, friends, and it leaves Hamor and Shechem with a choice to make.

The answer is delighted. The text says Shechem “…did not hesitate to fulfill this request, because he was delighted with Jacob’s daughter.” That's the reason the text gives, friends, and it's the only one it gives.

The answer is False. At the gate, Hamor and Shechem say, “These men are at peace with us. Let them live and trade in our land…” They speak of Jacob's family as men at peace, not as a danger. Back in verse 13, the text told us the sons had answered deceitfully.

The answer is True. Hamor and Shechem ask the men at the gate, “Will not their livestock, their possessions, and all their animals become ours?” That's part of the pitch, friends. They tell the men what they have to gain.
The answer is Simeon and Levi, Dinah's brothers. The text names them right there in verse 25. This is a heavy part of the story, friends, so let's take it slow.

The answer is their sister Dinah. The text says they “…took Dinah out of Shechem’s house, and went away.” The verse also names Hamor and Shechem, whom they killed with their swords. Dinah is the one they take out with them.

The answer is True. Verse 27 says Jacob's other sons “…came upon the slaughter and looted the city…” and then gives the reason: “…because their sister had been defiled.” That's the text's reason for it. Heavy stuff, friends.

The answer is children. The text says they “…carried off all their possessions and women and children…” The same verse says they plundered everything in their houses. That's a heavy line, friends, and I think it hits hard.

The answer is that the people of the land might unite and attack his household. That's Jacob's fear. He says, “We are few in number; if they unite against me and attack me, I and my household will be destroyed.” He's counting heads, friends, and the numbers don't look good to him.

The answer is that they ask if Shechem should have treated their sister like a prostitute. They reply, “Should he have treated our sister like a prostitute?” The text doesn't say they're sorry and doesn't say they promise anything. They answer their father with a question.
